events.title: Sysmon Event 1 — Process creation

overview.summary: Records creation of a new process with execution context including full command line, stable ProcessGuid correlation, configured image hashes, logon/session context and parent-process details.
security_value: reconstruct process creation and parent/child execution chains
correlate process activity across Sysmon events with ProcessGuid
investigate suspicious command lines, executable paths and integrity context
pivot from process execution to network, DNS, image-load and process-access telemetry

requirements: Sysmon must be installed and running.
The active Sysmon EventFiltering configuration must not exclude the ProcessCreate activity required by the investigation.
collection.configuration_note: ProcessCreate is a filterable Sysmon event. Collection volume and exclusions should be governed for the environment without removing required security visibility.
collection.hash_note: Image hashes reflect the hash algorithms configured for Sysmon and may contain multiple algorithm/value pairs.

correlations.purpose: network activity attributed to the created process
process termination and lifetime
image/module load context when ImageLoad is enabled
process-access context
DNS query context
parent/child process-chain reconstruction
Windows process-creation corroboration
correlations.limitation: Windows can reuse PIDs; ProcessGuid is preferred within Sysmon and time/context are required for cross-provider correlation

analysis: Review unusual parent/child chains, script interpreters, LOLBins and execution from user-writable or temporary paths.
Inspect full command lines, image metadata, configured hashes, user/logon context and integrity level together rather than treating any single field as a malicious verdict.
Use ParentProcessGuid and ProcessGuid to reconstruct execution lineage, then pivot to network, DNS, image-load and process-access telemetry where available.
Treat file-version metadata such as Company, Product, Description and OriginalFileName as contextual claims from the executable metadata, not proof of trust.

events.title: Sysmon Event 2 — A process changed a file creation time
aliases: A process changed a file creation time
events.source_locator: Events > Event ID 2: A process changed a file creation time

overview.summary: Records a process changing a file creation timestamp and preserves both the new and previous UTC creation times with process identity for investigation.
security_value: identify file creation-time changes that may indicate timestomping or anti-forensic activity
attribute timestamp changes to a stable Sysmon process identity
compare new and previous creation times during file-system timeline reconstruction
correlate timestamp changes with process creation and related file activity

requirements: Sysmon must be installed and running.
The active Sysmon EventFiltering configuration must not exclude the FileCreateTime activity required by the investigation.
collection.interpretation_note: Legitimate applications can modify file creation times. Collection and analysis should preserve process and surrounding file activity so timestamp changes are not treated as a malicious verdict by themselves.

correlations.purpose: process creation and execution context for the process changing the timestamp
related file creation or overwrite activity
related file deletion activity where those event classes are collected
Windows process-creation corroboration
correlations.limitation: PID values can be reused; ProcessGuid is preferred inside Sysmon

analysis: Compare CreationUtcTime with PreviousCreationUtcTime and the surrounding file-system timeline to identify suspicious backdating or other anomalous timestamp changes.
Use ProcessGuid to pivot to the process creation record and related Sysmon activity before deciding whether the timestamp change is suspicious.
Prioritize timestamp changes made by unusual processes, script interpreters, LOLBins or executables from user-writable locations, while accounting for legitimate software behavior.
Treat Event 2 as observation telemetry rather than a malicious verdict.

Treat Event 3 as observation telemetry, not a malicious verdict.

correlate service-state changes with configuration changes, errors and surrounding host activity

identify nearby Sysmon internal errors that may explain telemetry disruption
review process execution around unexpected service-state transitions

analysis: Establish whether the reported state change aligns with an approved reboot, upgrade, maintenance window or administrative action.
Investigate unexpected stops or repeated restart patterns because they can reduce host telemetry visibility, while avoiding treating the event alone as proof of tampering.
Record Version and SchemaVersion when comparing telemetry behavior across hosts or before and after upgrades.

events.title: Sysmon Event 5 — Process terminated

overview.summary: Records termination of a process and preserves stable process identity and execution context so analysts can complete process timelines and correlate related Sysmon activity.
security_value: complete process execution timelines by pairing process termination with process creation
identify short-lived or unexpectedly terminating processes when surrounding context warrants investigation
correlate the terminated process with other Sysmon telemetry through ProcessGuid
support duration and lifecycle analysis without treating normal process exit as a malicious verdict

requirements: Sysmon must be installed and running.
The active Sysmon EventFiltering configuration must not exclude the ProcessTerminate activity required by the investigation.
collection.configuration_note: ProcessTerminate is a filterable Sysmon event. Exclusions should be governed so required lifecycle visibility is preserved.
collection.interpretation_note: Process termination is routine operating-system activity. Event 5 provides lifecycle evidence and should be interpreted with process creation and surrounding telemetry rather than as a malicious verdict by itself.

correlations.purpose: pair process creation and termination to reconstruct process lifetime
review network activity associated with the process before termination
review DNS activity associated with the process before termination

analysis: Pair Event 5 with Sysmon Event 1 using ProcessGuid to reconstruct process lifetime and surrounding execution context.
Review unusually short-lived or repeatedly terminating processes only in conjunction with image path, user context, process creation data and related telemetry.
Use ProcessGuid as the preferred Sysmon correlation key because Windows process IDs can be reused over time.
Treat Event 5 as process-lifecycle observation telemetry rather than evidence of maliciousness by itself.

events.title: Sysmon Event 6 — Driver loaded

overview.summary: Records a kernel driver load with the loaded image path, configured hashes, and signature-related context for investigation of driver trust and kernel-level activity.

reconstruct driver-load timelines without treating a driver load as malicious by itself

collection.configuration_note: DriverLoad is a filterable Sysmon event. Include/exclude policy should preserve the driver telemetry required by the environment's detection and investigation objectives.
collection.interpretation_note: Driver loading can be legitimate administrative, operating-system, security-software, or application activity. Signature-related information is produced asynchronously by Sysmon, so signature context should be interpreted together with hashes, image path, time, and corroborating evidence rather than as a standalone malicious verdict.

analysis: Prioritize unexpected driver paths, unusual publishers/signature states, uncommon hashes, and driver loads temporally associated with suspicious installation or privilege activity.
Use ImageLoaded and Hashes to pivot into approved file reputation, inventory, or threat-intelligence evidence when available.
Correlate with Sysmon FileCreate or Windows service/driver telemetry when available, while preserving the fact that Event 6 itself does not identify the initiating user-mode process.
Treat Event 6 as high-value kernel driver observation telemetry, not proof of maliciousness by itself.

Use Hashes, Signature, SignatureStatus, Company, Product, OriginalFileName, and ImageLoaded together rather than treating any single metadata field as a malicious verdict.
Pivot by ProcessGuid to process creation, network, DNS, process-access, and lifecycle telemetry when those events are collected.

events.title: Sysmon Event 8 — CreateRemoteThread detected

collection.interpretation_note: Cross-process thread creation is security-relevant but is not intrinsically malicious. Legitimate debuggers, security products, instrumentation, and application components can perform similar operations.
collection.field_note: StartModule and StartFunction are inferred by Sysmon and may be empty when the start address is outside known loaded modules or exported functions.

fields.meaning: SID of the target account when the process runs in a different security context.
Target account name when creator and target contexts differ.
Domain or local-computer context of the target account.
Identifier of the target logon session when creator and target contexts differ.
fields.correlation: Use to correlate the target security context with session events.

fields.meaning: Hexadecimal PID assigned to the newly created process.
fields.correlation: Correlate with Event 4689 Process ID and other process-scoped telemetry; PID reuse requires time context.

fields.meaning: Full executable path of the newly created process.
Indicates whether the process token is full, elevated or UAC-filtered.
Mandatory Integrity Control label associated with the new process.
PID of the process that created the new process.
fields.correlation: Correlate with an earlier 4688 New Process ID to reconstruct parent/child lineage.

fields.meaning: Executable path of the parent/creator process.
Executable command line and arguments when command-line process auditing is enabled.
fields.notes: The field is commonly empty when the command-line inclusion policy is not enabled.
